content.thinking:
I need to carefully plan the whole file without being able to test run it. I'm designing a qilin as a quadruped with a deer-like body, dragon head, antlers, scaled hide, cloud-like mane, ox tail, and hooves, roughly 2.2m long and 2.1m tall at the head.

I'm settling on a high-fantasy anime toon style with cel shading and gold accents — a jade-teal scaled coat with cream belly, gold trim, pale cyan-white cloud swirl mane, gold-ivory antlers with glowing tips, amber glowing eyes, and gold hooves, plus hanging gold tassels. I need to be careful with coordinate conventions (mirroring left/right) and am now starting to lay out the skeleton, beginning with a hips root joint.

Working out the spine and neck chain positions, I'm mapping a catmull path from hips through chest to shoulders, then up into an arched neck leading to the head, trying to keep joint counts matching the number of spans so the chain structure resolves cleanly with the first spine joint effectively acting as the pelvis root.

Adjusting proportions so the neck ends a bit lower around 1.95 height, with antlers reaching up to about 2.5 for that mythic towering look. Now I'm setting up the leg joints, starting with the front shoulder position before building out the limb structure.

Continuing down through cannon bone to fetlock and hoof, with the knee bending forward as in real animals. Checking the geometry: shoulder height 1.15, segment lengths summing to 1.18, target foot height near 0.1 gives a vertical span of about 1.05, which is less than the total leg length so the leg will bend naturally. With three segments I need two inner bend directions, one at the elbow and one at the knee joint.

For the front leg specifically, I'm mapping humerus, forearm, and cannon segments with the elbow bending backward and the knee bending forward, keeping the cannon segment roughly parallel to the root-to-target line. Then I'll set up the hind leg similarly, with hip, stifle, hock, and fetlock joints using slightly different segment lengths.

Naming the chain joints shoulder, elbow, carpus, hoof for front legs with side suffix L/R, parenting front legs to spine3 and hind legs to hips. I'm treating the limb points as a polyline chain so the joints land exactly at the knots rather than smoothing through corners, then setting sweep radii for the leg silhouette.

For bulk at the shoulders and hips, I'll add extra sphere masses at those joint positions rather than relying solely on the loft width, giving the haunch and shoulder blade more volume.

Now I'm working out the hooves using small cylinder shapes with gold coloring, plus a torus ring at the fetlock and cloud-fur tufts for that qilin look, and calculating the exact vertical offset so the hoof sits correctly beneath the leg's end joint.

Simplifying the body loft to span from rump to chest using the hips and spine bones, letting the rump region fall under the first span's ownership before the spine chain takes over. Then moving on to sweep the neck chain with tapering radii.

Defining more loft stations...

Working out overall proportions now: body centered around y=1.2 with belly clearance near 0.9 for the long deer-like legs, back rising to about 1.55 at the withers, and neck/head extending up to roughly 2.0 with antlers reaching 2.45 — big like a large horse, but that fits the mythic Qilin scale.

I'm setting spine stations for the loft path so the body curve flows smoothly from tail to shoulders, then working out the coat shading — using countershaded jade scales with a cel-shaded paint layer on top for that stylized scale look.

Checking the texel density for scale size against the paint atlas resolution, I land on 2048px as a good balance between crispness and texture memory, since 4096 would be overkill given everything else packed into the atlas.

I'm working out the belly and dorsal coloring: a cream belly with a gold edge using a fur-edge effect oriented along the body's z-axis, plus a gradient on the legs that shifts to golden fur toward the lower limbs.

Now I'm settling on the final palette — jade greens for the main body, deep teal shadows, cream and gold accents for the belly and edges, and a pale cyan-white mane.

I'm setting up the scale texture with layered jade tones fading to a deep edge, plus a separate cream-and-gold scale pattern for the belly, then combining them with a fur-edge transition that has a toothed boundary and a thin golden ink outline.

Now I'm wrapping everything in a shading layer that resolves proper surface normals for lighting, and planning the neck coat to continue the same scale pattern with belly fur underneath and a mane running along the top. For the head, I'm thinking through a dragon-like deer design built from joints and swept geometry, working out the forward-facing orientation.

Defining head loft stations...

Wait, I realize the directional words refer to world axes, not bone-local axes, so I need a helper that translates left/along/up into the actual frame directions for a tilted head bone.

Now I'm working out the jaw joint as a child bone of the head, positioning it below the head's center and lofting its shape from wider near the hinge to narrower at the chin. I'm considering giving it a slight rest-pose rotation to open the mouth a bit, applied after the geometry is built so it stays rigidly attached.

Then I'm moving on to the eyes, planning to decal them onto the skull sphere surface near the front of the head.

I realize I can use frame: head to derive orientation directly from the head frame's quaternion, combined with an explicit `at` position, so {bone: head, frame: head, at: hp(...)} should work cleanly for placing head parts with scale [width, along, height].

Now I'm working out how to place the eyes as decals on the skull surface, using the hit point, outward direction, and a small size for the eye shape.

Now I'm planning out the full dragon head feature set: brow ridges, nostrils, flowing whiskers, a beard tuft, fangs, tongue, antler-horns, fin-like ears, cheek frills, and a glowing amber forehead gem decal. I'm thinking through the antlers specifically as branching, deer-style golden/ivory structures.

Writing antler geometry...

I'll add small glowing cyan spheres at the tine tips for a magical effect, then move on to designing the mane as cloud-like textured cards scattered along the neck, using a swirling wisp SVG shape with white fill and cyan/gold shading for the cloud curl texture.

Adding inner swirl details...

Actually, I think a simpler cloud-curl "ruyi" style texture would work better here—using two variants, a tall curling wisp and a rounded puff shape, then figuring out how to orient the mane cards flowing backward from the neck with some lean and bend.

Building mane points array...

Now I'm planning card placement along the neck rows at varying angles for scatter, plus additional tufts at the chest ruff, fetlocks, and tail. I'm also considering adding sculpted cloud-curl extrusions along the neck, shoulders, and flank to reinforce the qilin's flame/cloud silhouette.

Working out decal placement and orientation...

I'll just mirror the swirl regardless of side since it reads symmetric enough. Writing SVG spiral path for the gold ruyi cloud decal...

Now for the tail, I'm planning an ox/lion-style tail with a flame-cloud tuft: a chain of joints curving in an S-shape, with a ring of wisp cards clustered at the tail tip for a plume effect.

Still plotting tail chain points...

Checking overall proportions: antlers reach around 2.5 total height, tail peaks near 2.1. I'm verifying no geometry dips below the ground plane, confirming hoof placement sits right at zero, and checking that leg segment lengths are long enough to reach from shoulder to hoof target.

Hind legs need similar checking — root to target distance is about 1.1, with segment lengths summing to 1.34, giving enough slack for the hock to bend back naturally. I'm reasoning through how the solver will likely keep the cannon segment vertical while the upper two bones angle forward and back to form a believable hind-leg stance.

Now I'm mapping out the front leg geometry — elbow points back, carpus points forward, so the forearm hangs roughly vertical beneath the shoulder, matching real limb anatomy. I'm defining the chain root for the front leg at the shoulder joint position.

Naming the joints consistently: front legs get shoulder/elbow/carpus/hoof with L/R suffixes based on side, hind legs get hip/stifle/hock/hoof similarly, deriving the side letter from whether the x-coordinate is positive or negative. I'm also placing the shoulder joint attached to the spine and planning to add a small muscle bulge sphere near the shoulder for realism.

Skipping dew claws, but adding fetlock tufts as a ring of small wisp cards positioned near the hoof joint along the leg chain, oriented to flow downward with a steep lean so they drape off the fetlock naturally, sized and tinted in a gold-white tone.

I'm defining a separate flame-lick texture in cream-gold for the fetlock tufts rather than tinting the existing cyan-white wisp texture, planning three distinct textures total for cloud wisps, flame tufts, and whatever comes next.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry using an extrusion technique, defining an outline shape and orienting it along an outward-backward direction with approximate coordinates for a leaf-like fin ear.

Reworking the ear orientation so the flat face points forward-outward like deer ears, computing the cross product to confirm the plate normal works regardless of sign since it's a solid extrusion visible from both sides. Now I'm positioning the ear base relative to the head.

For the ear itself, I'm layering a second smaller extrude in a lighter color just inside the main ear shape with slightly more thickness so it pokes through on both faces without z-fighting, giving a simple inner-ear highlight. Since I can't visually iterate, I'm keeping proportions moderate but aiming for enough detail to look intentional.

Now I'm sketching additional head features for the dragon-qilin: a broad lion-like brow, cheek whiskers, chin beard, and a jaw horn, then adding a gold ornate collar with a bell around the neck by sweeping a loop cut from the neck tube surface at one of the neck joints.

Still writing collar details...

For the gold accent, I'm thinking of a chest band looped around the spine joint, cutting across the torso loft only so the legs stay unaffected, giving it a breastplate-like look—though maybe a flowing gold-rope sash with tassels fits the qilin's ornate style better than a rigid plate.

Now I'm detailing the sash: a thin gold rope loop around the waist with hanging tassel cards on each side, using vermilion ribbon accents for contrast. I'm also considering anime-style flourishes like a gold crescent mark on the forehead and layered dragon-scale plates along the shoulders and spine, built from small card or cone geometry to create a dorsal ridge effect.

Now I'm adding small gold dorsal spikes along the backbone like qilin flame fins, riding the body tube's frame orientation, plus chest tufts scattered near the front using position filters based on height and normal direction.

I'm also planning golden swirling cloud decals on the shoulders and haunches, and working out whisker placement as curved paths flaring outward and curling from points near the muzzle, computed in world-space coordinates off the nose position.

For the chin, I'm adding flame-textured beard cards hanging from the jaw, using frames oriented upward and flowing downward from attachment points at the jaw bone.

Now I'm working on fangs as small cones at the muzzle, pointing downward for the upper jaw and upward for the lower, colored cream and weighted to head/jaw bones. For the tongue, I'm thinking a simple flattened coral-colored box between the jaws will do since the mouth only opens slightly.

For the interior, I'll add a dark purple slab between the jaw and upper head to fake mouth darkness since no proper cavity geometry exists.

Then I'm adding small dark nostril spheres near the snout tip and rounding off the muzzle end for a dragon-like broad nose, plus sweeping brow ridges as curves from the eye area using a helper function that converts left/along/up offsets into head-local coordinates.

I'm placing the eyes on the sides of the skull ellipsoid using azimuth and elevation angles from the skull center, but I'm realizing the eye decals might end up hidden under the upper-head loft since the loft's width at that station could cover the same surface area.

I'm adjusting the eye placement angle further back to avoid the snout loft occluding them, then reconsidering a broader skull scale for a dragon-like brow so the loft stays narrower than the eye position at that station.

I'm checking decal projection against the skull surface and deciding the iris color should be a warm amber-gold to contrast against the jade body tone.

For facial texture I'm keeping the expressive brow stroke but turning off blush. For paint, I'll reuse the jade scale coat at a smaller scale size for the head, and share the body's cream belly paint for the underside of the lower jaw based on normal direction.

Defining scale patterns for the main coat and belly with jade and cream tones, then combining them with a cel-shaded fur edge that adds a gold ink outline where the two paints meet, which will interact with the cel shading's shadow resolution.

I'll avoid nesting cel calls by defining a raw coat layer once, then building the body from it directly and the legs from a gradient blend toward a gold scale-like tone. Checking texel density across the painted surface area confirms roughly 1.75mm resolution at 2048 texture size, which should be sufficient detail for the body coloring.

For the antlers, I'm thinking through a gradient from ivory at the base to gold at the tip, using banded color stops that can still be cel-shaded for the anime look while keeping the total flat-color palette under the limit.

I'll apply cel-shading broadly to big surfaces like horns and hooves for a toon two-tone look, but reserve flat colors for small glowing parts since glow effects can't live on painted cel materials. Mixing the two — cel for most visible geometry, flat colors for glow elements — keeps things cohesive while managing bake complexity.

I'm defining the gold, ivory, coral, and dark color sets as cel/flat fills, then checking that the sweep and ring-placement functions accept these fill types correctly for geometry without UVs.

Now I'm setting up the imports for the Qilin creature file, pulling in only the builder, path, paint, and toon/glow kit functions I actually use to avoid unused-import errors, before starting the exported meta object and main build code.

Writing SVG curl-cloud path...

Drawing the flame shape now...

Next I'm designing a tassel texture with a gold cord and vermilion tassel strands, thinking through how it should hang and orient when seen from downstream so the root edge appears on top.

Writing SVG code...

Building the skeleton rig now...

I'm adjusting the neck curve points to create a more dramatic swan-like arch, with the head bending forward at the poll for that classic horse silhouette, then chaining the neck joints off the spine's final joint.

Now I'm defining the head joint attached to the end of the neck chain, then adding a jaw joint with a helper function that converts local offsets into head-relative coordinates for positioning the jaw forward and up from the head's pivot.

Moving to the tail, I'm building a curved path through five points from the hips down and back up, splitting it into four tail segments (tail1-4) parented to the hips joint, with a tapering radius profile and a dark coat color for the sweep geometry.

Then for the legs, I'm setting up a mirrored loop over left/right sides, computing front limb joint positions from root to foot target with three bone lengths and bend directions for the two inner joints, expecting the limb helper to return the chain of joint points from root to end.

Next I'm creating the front leg chain parented to the correct spine joint with four named joints forming three spans, then working out how to key radius values for the sweep given the uneven bone lengths — trying to figure out whether five evenly spaced keys line up properly with the actual joint positions along the arc length.

Then I'm adding gold cuff ornaments at the fetlock using a torus rotated 90° about the X-axis so it wraps horizontally around the leg, positioning it using the chain's point-at-parameter lookup.

For the fetlock tuft, I'm using a ring generator to space out points around the leg at that joint, then feeding those into a card system with flame-colored, leaning geometry to create the hair tuft effect.

Now I'm adding the hoof itself as a tapered cylinder attached to the leg's tip joint, positioning it near the ground at the toe location.

Defining the hind limb chain...

Still writing body loft sections...

Then I'm verifying the belly height clears the legs at roughly .97 and that the shoulder position sits comfortably inside the body silhouette before moving to define the bone hierarchy list.

Building the skull sphere now, and working out the fur-edge cel shading for the head versus a lighter belly tone on the lower jaw, with some teeth/period parameters to control the shading pattern.

Now I'm defining the upper snout as a loft shape, laying out stations along the head bone with positions, widths, and heights that taper down toward the nose.

For the lower jaw, I'm plotting a similar sequence of loft stations along the jaw bone, checking widths and heights narrow appropriately toward the chin and that there's a proper gap between upper and lower jaw.

Adjusting the jaw positions more, I find a small gap near .34 where upper and lower meet with about .035 clearance, which looks right for a slightly open mouth. I'm adding a dark interior slab box positioned between the jaws to read as mouth shadow, visible through the gap. I'm second-guessing whether the lower jaw droops too much for a resting closed pose, but decide the gap plus an additional rotation for an open pose should work fine.

I'll skip the extra pose and keep just the gap, setting up the jaw joint bone with an aim target pointing down and forward from the skull. For teeth, I'm placing upper fangs as spikes anchored to the head bone pointing downward, and lower fangs anchored to the jaw bone pointing upward, both in an ivory color, then considering adding small rows of teeth along each side via a loop.

Now I'm adding nostril spheres on the head bone positioned near the snout tip, and sketching a gold nose ridge as a catmull sweep running from the forehead down to the nose bridge, checking it sits just above the loft geometry to avoid clipping.

Next I'm placing a small glowing forehead gem using an octahedron geometry with cyan glow, positioned centered above the skull near the forehead area, flattened slightly to sit against the surface.

Adding gold ring setting...

Now I'm starting the antler base construction, defining a function that builds each antler by positioning its base point offset laterally from center, symmetric for both sides.

Sketching the antler beam as a swept-back curve made of points moving outward, upward, and backward from the base.

Still writing tine geometry...

Adding gold torus rings...

Now for cheek frills: extruding a fin shape flaring outward from the cheek with a sharp dragon-fin outline, oriented so it faces sideways like a fish fin, with thickness and a gradient color from cyan to gold.

Good, no crossing edges, so I'll leave smoothing at default rather than forcing it to zero. Now I'm setting the cheek fin's cel color, then moving on to whiskers, beard, and mane cards, working out how the dorsal mane line follows the neck tube's sweep frames at each angle and position.

I'm thinking through the mane card placement rows—crest cards up top facing the up-normal, flanked by side rows at steeper angles—since the flow direction tips backward and down over the neck, but I realize standing cards oriented along that flow would appear edge-on from a side view, which isn't what I want for a mane that should read clearly from the side, so I need to reconsider how lean and bend affect the card's visible face.

Flattening that flow onto the crest's upward-normal plane puts width roughly along the back-forward axis, keeping it visible from the side. So the mane splits into left and right sets of rows, each with its own clockwise angle convention relative to the tube direction, defining which side each lock sits on.

Working through the flow vectors for each side with lean, bend, and sink values set, I check the texture orientation logic—since each side's flow direction points outward toward its own viewer, both sides read correctly as drawn rather than mirrored.

Now I'm verifying wisp hook direction by computing viewer "right" vectors using cross products of facing and up: for the left-side viewer, right maps to the model's back so the hook curls backward correctly, while for the right-side viewer, right maps to the model's front so the hook curls forward as intended.

I'm settling on roughly 72 mane cards total (two rows of 14 per side plus a 16-card crest), with varying sizes for crest versus upper/lower side rows, and randomizing cloud textures across them. I'm also sketching out additional forelock cards hanging from a frame positioned between the horns on the skull.

I'm skipping the forehead area to keep eyes visible, instead placing 3 cards per side behind the horns flowing backward over the poll, plus adding cloud puff cards scattered across the chest ruff area.

For the chest scatter, I'm working out the orientation math so the cards hang downward with their width facing front, and deciding to use cross-geometry (doubled, visible from all angles) for the chest, fetlocks, and tail tufts. I'm also considering adding flame wisp cards near the shoulders and hips.

Checking the card orientation math again: with lean at 70 degrees the spine tilts mostly toward the back, so the plane's normal ends up pointing roughly sideways, which means the card stays visible and flat when viewed from the side rather than vanishing edge-on.

For body-surface cards with steep lean they're face-on from outside, similar to feathers, while mane cards with shallower lean flowing outward still read reasonably from the side. I'm also noting that the scatter function accepts a filter callback that checks hit normals, and planning to add underside wisps near the neck and continue into the tail.

For the tail I'm setting up rings at several points along its length with varying card counts, radii, and sizes for a flame-like cloud effect, leaning the cards toward the tail's tangent direction flattened into the plane perpendicular to the outward normal so they flow naturally along the tail's curve.

Confirming ring() takes a chain point frame correctly, then thinking about gold ornaments on the body—placing a girth rope loop near the waist joint, and considering a flowing vermilion sash with gold trim cutting the body at that waist plane.

Now I'm working out the sweep geometry for the ribbon: closed loop path with a tube or box cross-section, worrying about which local axis defines the band's width versus thickness since parallel-transport frames make the orientation uncertain. I decide to simplify by using a circular rope cross-section instead, with the main gold rope plus two offset ropes to flank it.

Adding gold edge ropes alongside the band, then placing a gold knot sphere and hanging tassel cards at the left flank, angled and sized to drape naturally off the hit point.

Now I'm adding flowing ribbon streamers curving back from the knot with a vermilion sweep and scattered gold bead sprinkles, then sketching a gold collar loop around the neck with studs and a glowing pendant centerpiece.

For the gold ring I need to rotate the torus geometry so its axis aligns with the surface normal instead of standing up like a hoop, using rotateX on the geometry itself. I'm also double-checking that the hit point from the neck joint isn't null and that the joint's frame gives a valid center for the directional raycast.

Now I'm placing dorsal spikes along the body tube using a sweep function that samples points along the surface, orienting each spike outward with a gold color—simple fin spikes should read as anime-style without overcomplicating with flame-shaped extrusions. I'm also checking the seam where the body tapers into the tail, comparing radii at the loft boundary to make sure the transition looks smooth rather than abrupt.

Next I'm adding whiskers—two per side, built as thin tapered tubes following a flowing curve from near the face out and down, one gold and one pale cyan for contrast, shaping their path with offset points so they drape naturally. I'm also considering small flame-tuft cards positioned above the eyes as stylized eyebrows.

Now I'm working on the beard: chin and cheek tufts made from flame-shaped cards hanging from frames anchored under the jaw and along the cheek, spacing several along the chin line and checking their placement against the jaw's lower bound. Hooves and fetlocks are already set, so I'm moving on to adding swirl decals on the shoulder and haunch surfaces on each side of the body.

I realize the haunch sphere bulges out past the body's half-width, which means it's actually what's visible at that spot rather than the body surface itself -- so I need to target the decal onto the haunch sphere's surface instead, treating it as its own part.

I'm deciding to skip the flank stripe pattern but considering a jade spine fin hidden under the mane. For the eyes, I'm placing a decal on the skull surface using angular coordinates to position it correctly, and thinking about adding gold eyelid and brow ridge details for extra character.

Checking that `local()` and related helper methods return plain Vector3s as expected, and confirming the flow function signature for cards accepts the direction inputs I'm passing. I'm also noting which imports I'll need—THREE, builder utilities, frame, limb, and curve functions like catmull.

For the whiskers and beam paths, I'm using catmull with arrays of Vector3 points. For the streamers/ribbons coming off the sash, I'll use bezier curves, making sure to pass the hit object itself (rather than just its plain point) so the bone reference carries through for sweeping.

Now I'm working out the ribbon geometry at the sash knot, adding helper vectors offset from the knot position, and deciding whether to use a tube or box cross-section for a flat ribbon look.

Actually for a flank-hanging streamer I need it facing sideways, so I should set the `up` vector to lean the normal toward X, giving thickness along X and width running fore-aft so it reads properly from a side view. For colors I'll go with a vermilion/coral cel tone and flat end caps, skip the bell shape, and focus on gold details — anklets at the fetlock via a torus, plus maybe a cuff ring for extra flair.

I'm deciding against small torus rings at the knee/hock joints since the leg angle would throw off their orientation — better to skip those and stick with the hoof band and cannon ring for gold accents. Instead, I'll add small tuft/wisp card elements near the hock and front elbow, using tangent-aligned frames so they stand naturally along the bone direction.

Now I'm roughly tallying part counts: each leg contributes about 7 pieces (sweep, hoof, cuff, cards, elbow cards), times four legs plus haunch/shoulder and decal pieces, with the head adding around 35 and the antlers another 28 from branches, glow, and rings, plus roughly 8 mane card meshes.

Totaling tail, sash, spikes, and mane cards gets me to around 160 parts overall, well under the budget, so I could even add extra detail like leg scale plates without worrying. I'm keeping triangle counts moderate by using small side counts on sweeps and spheres, setting up colored antler bands, and confirming the rng seed is properly initialized before moving into eye animation.

I'm wiring up the eye texture with amber iris settings, double-checking that the cards color parameter and rng option naming won't collide with the imported function, and verifying the IK chain, joint types, and hoof geometry placements are all correctly typed and positioned front and back.

Now I'm checking the hoof clearance above the floor and tracing how the fetlock tuft cards hang and lean off the leg to make sure they stay just above ground level, then verifying the tail's position doesn't dip below the floor either.

Chest, beard, and whisker cards all clear the floor fine when I trace their drop distances from the body. Totaling up the overall proportions, the creature comes out around 2.5m tall and roughly 3.6m long including the tail — big, but fitting for a towering mythic presence.

Now I'm double-checking the API surface I'm relying on: that limb chains made from Vector3 arrays work as path inputs, that sweep accepts a radius array with a fill color and options, and that loft's bone option accepts the joint references I'm passing in for the hips and spine.

I'm also verifying the sash loops — using frame() to define the cutting plane and loop() to trace around the body surface — and confirming that sweeping a closed loop without an explicit bone falls back to averaged weights carried from the path itself.

For the gold dorsal spikes, I'm walking along the body with `along`, placing spike elements at each point with a fixed length, radius, and gold fill, checking the callback's point argument matches the expected input type from similar examples.

I'm limiting the along range so the spikes avoid the mane and tail ends, using the `from`/`to` options. Now I'm turning to texture generation via svg markup, and listing out the flat color palette I'll need—dark tones, tooth white, gem cyan, and a few whisker and eye accent colors.

Defining more palette values for a jade-themed variant with cream, gold, and vermillion accents, then setting up scale paint textures for the body and head using these colors with specific size and width parameters.

Still defining shader layers...

Building the build function...

Finishing the jaw joint, then building the neck tube sweep and mane cards with varying sizes, lean, and flow parameters across rows along the neck.

Placing poll and backhead card frames near the skull's top-back, adjusting the up-offset so the point sits just above the skull curve rather than floating too high. Still working out the sink depth relative to card length before moving to the neck underside beard cards.

I'm adding a chest ruff scatter and confirming the needed imports (animeEye, cel, furEdge, INK) are all in use, with INK doubling as a flat dark color. Now I'm sketching the girth band as a row of tubes along the belly, experimenting with z-positions, radius, and spacing to get the tube count and width right.

Then I'm placing gold trim edges at the outer bands and sketching the body's cross-section with a slight loop tilt. I'm also working out a knot detail on each flank using an `around(center).at(azimuth, elevation)` helper to position small sphere shapes symmetrically on both sides of the body.

For the knot's tassels I'm attaching cards near the nearest spine joint, sizing and angling them to hang downward with a slight flow and sink offset, mirrored on each side. Then I'm adding streamer ribbons flowing back and down from each knot point, using control points to curve them outward and checking that their endpoints land safely above the floor.

Writing bezier ribbon code...

Then I'll add a thinner gold variant ribbon, keep texture definitions inside the build function rather than module scope to avoid redundant creation, and block in a dark hoof cleft shape before moving to decal textures.

Now I'm starting the import statements and module setup for the final TypeScript file, being careful that every declared constant gets used to satisfy strict linting rules.

Adjusting the antler beam curve to splay outward more, giving it a lyre-like shape with wider angled offsets as it extends from the skull.

Adding more tine geometry...

I should type-annotate the outline array explicitly to avoid literal widening issues, and fix the fin's x-axis to be properly orthogonal to y. Now I'm sketching the ear outline shape with the same typed array approach...

Also working through the ear's local orientation vectors—making sure x and y stay perpendicular so the ears lean back and splay outward correctly without any axis misalignment.

Still deriving ear vectors...

Now I'm defining a smaller inner-ear outline with its own thickness and color, nested inside the outer ear shape, before moving on to cheek fins at the jaw sides and the brow detail.

For the brow I'm sweeping a curve above the eye using catmull-rom interpolation through points offset from the skull, deciding between gold, ivory, or jade for the ridge color, and checking the vertical placement so the brow sweep clears the eye socket without overlapping it.

Adjusting the brow sweep points inward so they hug the skull surface more closely, checking the math against the ellipsoid curve at each x position — close enough with the tube radius giving a little embedding tolerance. The eye sits properly below the brow now, so I can move on to final code writing including the mouth interior slab and fangs.

Placing the upper fangs at the snout's bottom edge angled slightly backward, and the lower fangs rising from the jaw top with shorter length — checking that the mouth gap still allows them to pass beside each other when closed. Skipping smaller teeth along the jaw for now and moving to the tongue placement.

I'm flattening a small sphere to sit on the lower jaw as the tongue, coral-pink colored, and deciding to skip extras like a nose ring, forelock cards, and a cloud base since they'd conflict with the floor contact. Now I'm starting to scatter points across the chest surface for a ruff detail.

Scattering flank wisps using filtered surface hits on either side, targeting the upper flank region near the shoulder/hip spheres.

I'll use cross cards for the flank wisps so they read well from any angle, around 36 cards total with the cloud textures and no mirroring—should look like fluffy anime cloud-fur without over-cluttering the dragon. Settling on returning the root node, then double-checking the cards API signature for textures and ring items before finalizing.

Now I'm sketching the tail using a Catmull-Rom chain off the hips with four tapering sweep segments, though I'm noting the tail base sits pretty far from the hip joint and want to make sure the parenting still makes sense.

Adding tuft cards along the tail at several points, orienting each ring's cards along the tail's tangent direction with size scaling and a leaning angle, cycling through cloud/flame textures, then capping it with a tip plume card at the very end.

Since those joints rotate with leg poses but are fine at rest, I'll use the spine joint bone for shoulders and hips for haunches instead, so decals inherit the rigid bone weights correctly. I'm working out the decal call signature, passing literal position and direction coordinates for mirrored placement, with the mirror side chosen by sign. Now I'm starting on the skull geometry for the eyes.

Adding eye decals and skull surface mapping...

Writing jaw and head loft geometry...

Writing whisker sweep code...

Still defining helper functions and scale-sized geometry, confirming the neck collar and jade scale details, then moving on to writing the cloud texture fill colors.

Checking that all imports and variables are actually used before finalizing the code.
